title: Diffusion Policy
definition: Uses denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) to generate robot action sequences. The forward process adds Gaussian noise over $T$ steps: $q(\mathbf{a}^t | \mathbf{a}^{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}^t; \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,\mathbf{a}^{t-1}, \beta_t \mathbf{I})$. The learned reverse process iteratively denoises: $p_\theta(\mathbf{a}^{t-1} | \mathbf{a}^t, \mathbf{o}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}^{t-1}; \mu_\theta(\mathbf{a}^t, t, \mathbf{o}), \sigma_t^2 \mathbf{I})$, conditioned on observations $\mathbf{o}$. Training minimizes: $$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{a}^0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \left[ \| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{a}^t, t, \mathbf{o}) \|^2 \right]$$ Naturally handles multimodal action distributions — can represent multiple valid ways to accomplish a task.
intuition: Imagine a sculptor starting with a rough block of marble (noise) and iteratively refining it into a statue (action sequence). Each denoising step adds detail. The key advantage over BC: if there are two valid ways to pick up a mug (left side or right side), diffusion can represent both modes instead of averaging them into an invalid middle path.
practical_example: Diffusion Policy for bimanual manipulation: 2-step observation history (images + proprioception) $\rightarrow$ U-Net-based diffusion model $\rightarrow$ predict 16-step action chunks. With DDIM sampling ($\eta = 0$, 10 denoising steps instead of 100), runs at 10Hz on a GPU. Outperforms BC by 20-40% on multi-modal manipulation tasks.
failure_mode: Inference too slow for reactive control: full DDPM requires $T = 100$+ denoising steps per action chunk. With DDIM acceleration, still 10-20 steps needed. Symptoms: robot moves in stop-and-go pattern due to inference latency. Fix: use DDIM with fewer steps (10), consistency distillation, or single-step generators. Also: noise schedule $\{\beta_t\}$ tuning is critical — wrong schedule produces either conservative (too low $\beta$) or jittery (too high $\beta$) actions.
interview_answer: Diffusion policies are the state-of-the-art for learning multi-modal manipulation behaviors. The key advantage: they naturally represent multiple valid action modes without mode averaging. Architecture: observation encoder $\rightarrow$ conditioning $\rightarrow$ U-Net denoising network predicting $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{a}^t, t, \mathbf{o})$ $\rightarrow$ action chunks. In practice: DDIM with 10 steps is fast enough for 10Hz control. Combine with action chunking (predict 16 steps) for temporal consistency. The main trade-off vs BC: higher quality but slower inference and harder to train. I see diffusion policies as the default for manipulation tasks with multi-modal behavior (assembly, tool use, bimanual).

title: Flow Matching for Action Generation
definition: Flow matching learns a continuous-time vector field $v_\theta(\mathbf{x}, t)$ that transports samples from a simple distribution $p_0 = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ to the target distribution $p_1$ (actions). The trajectory follows the ODE: $\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = v_\theta(\mathbf{x}, t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. Conditional flow matching (CFM) enables efficient training by regressing to the conditional vector field: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, q(\mathbf{x}_1)} \left[ \| v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) - (\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0) \|^2 \right]$$ where $\mathbf{x}_t = (1-t)\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{x}_1$ is the linear interpolation path. Simpler training than diffusion (no noise schedule), faster inference (fewer ODE solver steps).
intuition: Imagine a river that flows from a random starting point to exactly where you need to go. Flow matching learns the current of this river — given any point in the flow, it tells you which direction to move. Compared to diffusion (which adds and removes noise), flow matching directly learns the transport map. Simpler math, faster in practice.
practical_example: $\pi_0$ (Physical Intelligence): uses flow matching to generate robot action sequences from observations. Trains on large-scale multi-task robot data. Generates 50-step action chunks using an ODE solver (Euler or Dopri5) with 5-10 integration steps. Achieves real-time control at 15Hz. Architecture: pre-trained VLM backbone $\rightarrow$ flow matching action head conditioned on visual + language tokens.
failure_mode: ODE solver instability: the learned vector field $v_\theta$ may have regions where the flow is poorly defined (large Lipschitz constant), causing numerical issues. Symptoms: occasional action jumps or NaN outputs. Fix: use adaptive ODE solvers (Dopri5), train with flow regularization $\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \mathbb{E}[\|\nabla_\mathbf{x} v_\theta\|^2]$, clip extreme vector field values during inference.
interview_answer: Flow matching is emerging as a cleaner alternative to diffusion for robot action generation. The advantage: simpler training objective (regress to the conditional vector field $v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) \approx \mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_0$), faster inference (5-10 ODE steps vs 20-100 diffusion steps), and no noise schedule to tune. $\pi_0$ from Physical Intelligence shows this works at scale for multi-task robot control. Compared to diffusion policies, flow matching offers similar multimodality with simpler training and faster inference. I expect flow matching to become the default generative approach for robot control.

title: Multi-Modal Action Distributions
definition: When multiple valid action sequences exist for the same observation (e.g., reaching left or right around an obstacle). A single Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ collapses modes by averaging. Solutions: (1) Gaussian mixture models: $p(a|o) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(a; \mu_k, \Sigma_k)$; (2) Conditional VAEs: $p(a|o) = \int p(a|z,o)\, p(z|o)\, dz$ with latent $z$ selecting the mode; (3) Diffusion/flow matching: implicit multi-modal density through iterative refinement from noise.
intuition: Asked to go around a table, you can go left or right — both are correct. A single Gaussian averages these into 'go straight through the table.' Multi-modal methods represent both options and commit to one during execution. This is why diffusion policies work so well for manipulation — real tasks have many valid solutions.
practical_example: Block stacking: the gripper can approach from any direction. BC with MSE loss $\mathcal{L} = \|a - \hat{a}\|^2$ averages all approach angles $\rightarrow$ hovers above block without committing. Diffusion policy samples one valid approach direction each time $\rightarrow$ clean, committed trajectories with varying approach angles across rollouts.
failure_mode: Mode collapse: the model learns only one of multiple valid modes, losing diversity. In VAEs: KL term overpowers reconstruction $\rightarrow$ posterior collapses to prior ($q(z|x) \approx p(z)$). In diffusion: insufficient model capacity or training $\rightarrow$ converges to dominant mode. Symptoms: always takes the same approach despite multiple valid options. Fix: increase model capacity, use $\beta$-VAE scheduling ($\beta: 0 \rightarrow 1$ during training), ensure diverse training data.
interview_answer: Multi-modal action distributions are the fundamental reason why diffusion/flow matching policies outperform simple BC for manipulation. The problem: many real tasks have multiple valid solutions, and MSE-loss BC averages them into invalid actions. Solutions ranked by expressiveness: (1) Gaussian mixture models $\sum_k \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)$ — simple but limited modes, (2) CVAEs — flexible but training can be tricky, (3) diffusion/flow matching — most expressive, handle arbitrary distributions. In practice, the choice depends on real-time requirements: GMMs for fast control ($\sim 1000\,\text{Hz}$), diffusion for complex manipulation ($\sim 10\,\text{Hz}$).

title: Consistency Models for Single-Step Action Generation
definition: Consistency models learn a function $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$ that maps any point along a diffusion trajectory directly to the clean sample $\mathbf{x}_0$, enforcing the self-consistency property: $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) = f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t'}, t')$ for all $t, t'$ on the same trajectory. Can be trained via consistency distillation from a pre-trained diffusion model: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CD}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0} \left[ d\big(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1}),\; f_{\theta^-}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_n}, t_n)\big) \right]$$ where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t_n}$ is one DDIM step from $\mathbf{x}_{t_{n+1}}$, $\theta^-$ is the EMA target, and $d$ is a distance metric (e.g., LPIPS or $L_2$). Also trainable from scratch via consistency training (CT) without a teacher model.
intuition: Diffusion models are like taking 100 small steps from noise to a clean action — accurate but slow. A consistency model learns to take a single giant leap from any noise level directly to the final answer. Like training a student who, instead of solving every intermediate step of a math problem, learns to jump straight to the answer. The trade-off: slightly less precise, but 10-100x faster.
practical_example: Consistency Policy (Prasad et al.): distill a pre-trained diffusion policy into a consistency model for real-time robot control. Original diffusion policy: 10 DDIM steps at 50ms = 500ms per action chunk. Consistency model: 1-2 steps at 50ms = 50-100ms. On Push-T and robotic manipulation benchmarks: achieves $> 95\%$ of the diffusion policy's success rate with $5\text{-}10\times$ faster inference. Enables 20Hz+ closed-loop control on hardware with a single forward pass.
failure_mode: Quality gap: single-step generation is inherently less precise than multi-step refinement, especially for high-dimensional action spaces. The distilled model may struggle with the tails of the action distribution (rare but valid modes). Symptoms: slightly lower success rate on tasks requiring high precision (e.g., peg insertion with $< 1\,\text{mm}$ tolerance). Fix: use 2-4 step inference as a compromise (still much faster than full diffusion), train with larger model capacity, use progressive distillation schedule.
interview_answer: Consistency models solve the key deployment bottleneck of diffusion policies: inference speed. By learning to map any noise level directly to the clean sample (self-consistency property $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) = f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t'}, t')$), we get single-step generation. For robotics: this means going from 10+ denoising steps ($\sim 500\,\text{ms}$) to 1-2 steps ($\sim 50\text{-}100\,\text{ms}$), enabling real-time closed-loop control. The training recipe: take a well-trained diffusion policy, distill with consistency loss using EMA target network. I see consistency models as the deployment form of diffusion policies — train with diffusion for quality, deploy with consistency for speed.

title: Energy-Based Models for Robot Control
definition: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a policy implicitly through an energy function $E_\theta(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{o}): \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ where low energy corresponds to good actions. The policy distribution is: $$p_\theta(\mathbf{a} | \mathbf{o}) = \frac{\exp(-E_\theta(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{o}))}{Z_\theta(\mathbf{o})}, \quad Z_\theta(\mathbf{o}) = \int \exp(-E_\theta(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{o}))\, d\mathbf{a}$$ Action inference requires sampling from this distribution, typically via Langevin dynamics: $\mathbf{a}_{k+1} = \mathbf{a}_k - \frac{\lambda}{2} \nabla_\mathbf{a} E_\theta(\mathbf{a}_k, \mathbf{o}) + \sqrt{\lambda}\, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k$. Training uses contrastive divergence or noise contrastive estimation (NCE) to avoid computing the intractable partition function $Z_\theta$.
intuition: Instead of directly telling the robot what to do (explicit policy), an EBM defines a landscape over all possible actions — valleys are good actions, mountains are bad ones. The robot finds good actions by rolling a ball downhill on this landscape (gradient descent). The beauty: the landscape can have multiple valleys (multi-modal), and you can combine landscapes by addition (compositionality). Want an action that's both safe AND efficient? Just add the two energy functions.
practical_example: Implicit Behavioral Cloning (Florence et al.): instead of regressing $a = f_\theta(o)$, train an energy function $E_\theta(a, o)$ with InfoNCE loss: $\mathcal{L} = -\log \frac{\exp(-E_\theta(a^+, o))}{\exp(-E_\theta(a^+, o)) + \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{neg}}} \exp(-E_\theta(a_j^-, o))}$ where $a^+$ is the demonstration action and $a_j^-$ are negative samples. At inference: draw $N = 16384$ uniform action samples, evaluate energy on all, keep top-$k$, refine with Langevin dynamics. Achieves state-of-the-art on precise insertion tasks where multi-modal action distributions matter.
failure_mode: Sampling is expensive: Langevin dynamics requires many gradient steps through the energy network to find low-energy actions. For high-dimensional action spaces, MCMC mixing is slow. Symptoms: inference latency too high for real-time control, or sampler gets stuck in local minima (wrong mode). Fix: use derivative-free optimization (CEM + energy ranking), amortize sampling with a learned proposal network $q_\phi(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{o})$ trained to approximate $p_\theta$, or use EBMs only for scoring/reranking actions proposed by a faster generator.
interview_answer: EBMs offer a fundamentally different approach to robot control: instead of learning a direct mapping $o \rightarrow a$, learn a scoring function $E_\theta(a, o)$ over the action space. The advantages: (1) natural multi-modality — multiple low-energy valleys, (2) compositionality — combine energy functions for different objectives by addition, (3) flexible conditioning — easy to add constraints as additional energy terms. The main challenge is inference speed: sampling from $p(a|o) \propto \exp(-E_\theta(a,o))$ requires iterative optimization. In practice, I use EBMs in a reranking setup: fast generator proposes $N$ candidates, EBM scores them. This gets the best of both worlds — speed from the generator, quality from the energy model. Implicit BC showed this works well for precision tasks like insertion.
